fields.description:
## Context / Problem
PS5 code-review (advisory, edge-cases) on RP-05 S2a change 1925 found that
`rebar._cli._registry.route_for()` resolves only canonical route names (via the
`_BY_NAME` index) and returns `None` for any alias spelling. The `Route.aliases`
field is validated (no collisions with live canonical names, no duplicates, no
retired-name collisions — see `_check_duplicates` / `_check_alias_retired` at
`src/rebar/_cli/_registry.py:667-700`) but the registry offers no way to resolve
an invocation typed as an alias to its owning `Route`. The execution-dispatch
cutover needs `route_for` to be the authoritative resolver, so it must accept an
alias and return the owning route.

## Approach
Extend `route_for` to consult an alias index in addition to the existing
`_BY_NAME` index, with **canonical names taking precedence over aliases**.
Concretely, add a small pure `_index(routes)` helper that returns
`(by_name, by_alias)` where `by_alias` maps each alias of every **non-retired**
route to that route (retired routes are unrouted, so their aliases must not
resolve — mirrors `derive_policy_sets`'s live-only filter). Build the module-level
`_BY_NAME`/`_BY_ALIAS` from `ROUTES` once via `_index`. `route_for(spelling)`
returns `by_name.get(spelling)` first, falling back to `by_alias.get(spelling)`,
so a canonical spelling always wins over an alias (validation already forbids an
alias colliding with a live canonical name, so this is defensive precedence, and
it never resolves to a retired route). Add an optional `routes=ROUTES` parameter
(mirroring the existing `derive_policy_sets(routes=ROUTES)` pattern at
`src/rebar/_cli/_registry.py:635`) with a `routes is ROUTES` fast-path reusing the
prebuilt indexes, so callers and tests can resolve against a synthetic table
without a per-call rebuild on the hot dispatch path.

This is portable: the resolver is pure in-process logic over the route table with
no CI-provider or external-service trigger.

## Scope
- `src/rebar/_cli/_registry.py` — add `_index` helper; build `_BY_NAME`/`_BY_ALIAS`
  from it; extend `route_for` to fall back to the alias index with name precedence
  and accept an optional `routes` table. Kept well under the 800-LOC module cap
  (currently 770) and within the per-function complexity ceiling (route_for stays
  a trivial two-lookup function).
- `tests/unit/test_cli_registry.py` — add tests for alias resolution and precedence.

## Testing
Leaf, adds behavior. RED→GREEN unit tests in `tests/unit/test_cli_registry.py`:
- Happy path: `route_for("<alias>", routes=<synthetic table>)` returns the owning
  `Route` whose `aliases` contains that spelling.
- Precedence: when a spelling is a canonical name of one route and an alias of
  another route in the table, `route_for` returns the **canonical** owner.
- Retired: an alias declared by a `retired=True` route does **not** resolve
  (returns `None`), matching the unrouted contract.
- Regression: the shipped table (no aliases today) still resolves canonical names
  and returns `None` for unknown spellings; import-isolation is preserved.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `route_for` resolves an alias to its owning `Route`; verified by a new unit
      test in `tests/unit/test_cli_registry.py` that passes a synthetic table with
      an aliased route and asserts the returned route's `name`.
- [ ] Canonical names take precedence over aliases; verified by a unit test where a
      spelling is both a canonical name and another route's alias and `route_for`
      returns the canonical owner.
- [ ] A retired route's aliases do not resolve (`route_for` returns `None`);
      verified by a unit test.
- [ ] No regression: `make lint`, `make typecheck`, and
      `pytest tests/unit/test_cli_registry.py` all pass; the module stays ≤800 LOC
      and the complexity ratchet (`scripts/check_complexity_baseline.py --check`)
      reports no `new>0`/`increased>0`.
